posts.name: Paptimus
posts.cooked:
For me, it's very important that the storyline keeps some "holes" in it, in order to stay true to SotM nature as a game. I want to get enough "missing" narrative space to fill in the holes according to how my plays unfold. And speculation is almost always better (and once again, even more fitting for a game) than a definite fixed, completely written storyline.

I remember, when I was young and I would speculate about the origins of Wolverine (is he immortal? Did he lose his memory? When?) or Gambit (the lost Summers brother?)... Then the story was told, and those characters lost a lot of their aura to me. I couldn't "make them mine" as I used to, and I was almost condemned to stick to their "true" origins.

I think Christopher and Adam have done a masterful work until now of giving hints and pieces of the "true storyline", while keeping enough mystery for the game itself to unfold as a support for our own "version" of it.

I disagree with this, but I suspect that the disagreement is over the definition of 'canon' rather than anything in stoy.

I would say that Young Legacy and Legacy's incap sides are both canon.  I understand 'canon'  to mean anything that officially happened in the overarching Sentinels of the Multiverse story, whether or not it happened in the main timeline.  Both those incapacitations were made to have not-happened, but they're still part of the Sentinels story - if they hadn't existed at some point, the Sentinel's story would have happened differently.

I hope that makes sense, because my ability to use tenses in an understandable manner will be starting to break down.

posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
It depends on what theory of time and reality we ascribe to, and what kind of Multiverse the Multiverse is.

It is possible that everything is canon, because whatever could happen happened at some point, in one part of the multiverse.

 

For my use of canon, I'm thinking of the storyline of the card game, in which the Young Legacy incap was from the Iron Legacy timeline, and the Legacy incap is what should have happened before time was disrupted and reality changed.

Except that canon isn't a timeline concept - it's a narrative concept.  And Young Legacy's incap happened as part of the Sentinels narrative, even though it's no longer part of the timeline.

This is why time travel and alternate realities give people headaches.

 

Or to put it another way, I use 'canon' to mean anything that has appeared in a Sentinels comic (or would have appeared in a Sentinels comic if those comics existed).

Reminds me of Shepherd Book from Firefly.  His past was alluded to at various points, but the blanks weren't filled in.  The possibilities conjured up by the hints seemed so intriguing that I felt explicitly describing his past would always be a let-down, so I was glad they didn't do that.  Years later, I saw they'd put a comic out about his past.  "Oh wow," thought I, "this must be really good, because there's no way Mr. Whedon would break all that mystery unless he'd thought of a way to make the revelation really interesting and satisfying."  It was not.  It was disappointly poor.  If I could unread it, I would (and I recommend that no one reading this reads it). I don't expect Christopher to make that mistake (though, frankly, I didn't expect Joss Whedon to let his brother write such an awful comic either).

There's a variety of levels. Here's my thoughts (in the order they should probably be read):

  1. Better Days - Interesting and well-written, the characterizations were dead-on. I liked it a lot.
  2. Those Left Behind - Wonderfully smart and interesting, well-written, and good characterizations. I really enjoyed it.
  3. The Other Half - It was short and decently done, I thought, albeit a little jumbled. (It's available online.)
  4. Downtime - Another short one, but I thought it was fun (and available online).
  5. The Shephard's Tale - While it wasn't as great as I'd hope, very little ever is. :wink: Having said that, I thought it was very well done. I especially enjoyed the structure of it, and I found the story interesting and the writing pretty good (although I have some issues with plot holes).
  6. Float Out - I recommend skipping it. The only thing worth seeing is the last panel of the book. Just my opinion, of course - others might disagree.
  7. It's Never Easy - I didn't like the art, but the writing was okay. Not that impressive, in general, but entertaining enough (and, since it's available online, worth the price of admission).
I think that's all of them...
metlarcturus:

Also, I love dramatic mystery; the speculation really does end up being better than a reveal most of the time.

That, I think, is what hurt The Shephard's Tale the most. There were a lot of expectations and folks had their preferred theories. When those theories didn't pan out (as they rarely do), there was a lot of disappointment.

arenson9:

I enjoyed it.

Hey, some people must.  It has a 3 1/2 star average on Amazon, after all.  I'd say it probably helped if you didn't have very high expectations.  As I said above, I expected something amazing, because I thought that the wonderful sense of mystery wouldn't be stripped away if it wasn't to be replaced by a superbly-written backstory.  What I saw was less interesting than anything I'd imagined, which is part of why I call it poor (though not the only reason, but I shouldn't go on at greater length about it here).

To get back to the comment to which I originally responded, and thus move things back on-topic, it could just be that some people find mysteries more appealing than others.  I think there's an important balance to strike between leaving everything so vague that one doesn't have any interesting concrete details at all and filling in so many gaps that there's no longer room for imaginative speculation.  The way Christopher writes the characters of Sentinel Comics, we see plenty of tantalising story elements, but huge gaps are left that allow for tons of speculation.  Even when he finishes telling us everything that he wants to tell us, I hope some gaps will still be left, spaces in which we can put any of the games we play, imagining realistic reasons for why those encounters would occur.
